description: We are Adriana Ferrandino and Guillermo Sardón. Before humans return to the Moon or build a Mars base, where on Earth can we rehearse? Guillermo, an IT consultant and Systems Lab at UTN Bs As, built the data pipeline, cloud setup and AI workflow. Adriana, a logistics professional and amateur astronomer who searches for asteroids and studies radio astronomy. Our team is curious, committed and focused on making space exploration more efficient and resource-conscious.
summary: Celestial Analog Finder is an interactive map that finds and characterizes new places on Earth that resemble future landing sites and permanent bases on the Moon and Mars. Using open NASA data (MODIS temperature, albedo and land cover) together with the Copernicus elevation model, TerraClimate climate, and global geology and volcano catalogs, it scores all 337,611 land cells of the planet. Users choose a world, a mission (landing site, permanent base, or both side by side), and the characteristics that matter: terrain, geology, temperature, aridity, ice, volcanic caves, surface brightness and sunlight. The map updates instantly. Each candidate shows its score, the measured values with their sources, what it can be used to test, and what Earth cannot reproduce: gravity, vacuum and radiation. The system compares locations already used in simulations with new, as-yet-undiscovered locations; you can evaluate them for use as landing sites, bases, or both. That matters because analog campaigns keep returning to the same few famous sites. Our tool opens the whole planet to cheaper, closer test sites for the crews and machines that will go next.
details:
What it does

Celestial Analog Finder is a free web map that answers one question for mission planners, researchers and educators: where on Earth can we rehearse a specific Moon or Mars mission? The user picks a world (Moon or Mars), a mission type (landing site, permanent base, or both side by side) and a reference target: one of NASA’s Artemis III landing regions, a lunar base or cave site, or a key Mars landing or base target. They then choose which characteristics matter and how much. The map ranks every candidate on Earth instantly and shows the ten best distinct places.

How it works

We divided Earth’s land surface into 337,611 cells of 0.25°.

Using Google Earth Engine, we measured eight characteristics in every cell:

Topography: slope and relief, from the Copernicus 30 m elevation model.

Thermal regime: from NASA MODIS land surface temperature.

Surface brightness: albedo, from NASA MODIS.

Aridity: from TerraClimate.

Ice and polar conditions.

Geology: global lithology map (GLiM).

Volcanic terrain and caves: Smithsonian volcano catalog.

Illumination: computed from solar geometry.

The reference values for each Moon and Mars target are compiled from published NASA mission products and peer-reviewed papers, each with its citation.

Each characteristic is compared using the rule that fits it: absolute difference, requirement, climate regime or category. The selected characteristics are combined with a weighted geometric mean, so a site must be similar on everything that matters, not just one feature.

Built-in safeguards:

Missing data lowers a “coverage” indicator instead of counting as zero.

Hard limits remove a cell, for example slopes above 12° for a landing.

Only bare surfaces qualify (rock, sand, ice or sparse shrubland), so dark forests are never mistaken for lunar soil.

Each candidate opens a profile card that shows:

its score per characteristic and the measured values with units and sources;

the activities it could support (hazard avoidance, habitat construction, ice extraction, power systems in extreme light);

an honest list of what Earth cannot reproduce: gravity, vacuum, radiation and the lunar day–night cycle.

A short AI-written interpretation is pre-generated for the top candidates. A deterministic checker rejects any text containing a number that does not appear in the measured data.

Validation

We did not tell the engine which places are already used as analogs. When we ranked all land on Earth, recognized analog sites used in past simulations appeared in the top few percent for the missions they are known for. Landing and base rankings share no place in their top ten, which confirms they need different terrain. The top ten stays stable when any weight changes by ±20%.

Benefits and impact

Analog campaigns keep returning to the same few famous sites, which are often remote and expensive to reach. Our tool opens the whole planet to that search, revealing closer, cheaper and more diverse test sites. It is useful for:

space agencies and universities planning field tests;

rover and habitat teams looking for the right terrain;

teachers who want to show students what the Moon and Mars are really like.

Because it is transparent about sources and limits, it supports decisions instead of replacing them.

Tools and technologies

Python, Google Earth Engine, pandas and Parquet for the data pipeline.

React, Vite and MapLibre GL with OpenStreetMap for the dashboard, published as a static site on GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions. No login and no server costs.

An LLM (gpt-oss-120b on Groq) for the cached interpretations.

AI coding assistants (Google Antigravity, Claude, IBM Bob) for planning, implementation and review, all checked by the team.

ElevenLabs voices for the demo narration.

Creativity

Instead of a fixed list of “best analogs”, we turned the search into a mission question that anyone can tune. The same planet gives different answers for a landing and for a base, and for the Moon and for Mars. Every score can be traced back to a measurement and a source.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: what Earth cannot simulate, missing data and confidence levels are always shown.

Traceability of every number.

Robustness: weight stability and validation without bias.

Global coverage instead of a single region.

Accessibility: a free, fast and mobile-friendly site.

Compliance with the challenge rules on open data, AI disclosure and NASA branding.
